full_judgment:
5. Defendant No. 2 alone contested the suit by filing a written statement. His case, in short, is that the suit land was within Ramchandrapur hat of the erstwhile 'Zaminder.' With the wholesale acquisition of land receiving interest under section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 the suit land vested in the government. RS record of rights accordingly recorded the suit land as khas of the government. The suit land was situated at the periphery of Ramchandrapur Bazaar. By purchase from persons who had no title the plaintiff acquired no right title or interest in the suit land. Husband of the plaintiff got the suit land mutated in collusion with corrupt 'Tahshilder' and such mutation had no legal effect. 

 12. The plaint case is that the suit land originally belonged to one Tamej Sheikh and CS record of rights was accordingly, prepared in his name. CS Khatian No. 315, Exhibit 1 recorded the suit land comprising of CS plot No. 828 as 'Nal'. Nature of tenancy was recorded as 'Borga Korfa' under land receiver Durga Sundari Basu and others. The appellant Court took the view that such tenancy held as 'Barga Korfa' had no 'raiyati' right, had no right to transfer before the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 came into force. He however, did not mention any law or authority in support of his view. 

 13. Before the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 (Act Vlll of 1885) was in force. It was the law of landlord and tenant. Under said law different classes of interest in land were created. As different classes of landlord were created so the interest of the tenant was classified in various categories. 'Korfa' right was recognised as a kind of tenancy. A 'Korfa' tenant was not necessarily an under-raiyat of a raiyat. He was a sub-lessee of a 'Talukdar' or of a raiyat. Such right was made heritable and transferable, sometimes subject to some conditions. 

 22. Recording of the suit land as 'Chandina' in SA record of rights might have created all problems for the appellate Court. Such record was prepared sometime in 1964. With the wholesale acquisition of rent receiving interest, all land "in a hat or bazaar" vested in the government with effect from 2 April, 1956. But under sub-section 3 of section 44  of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 such land would stand finally acquired and vested in the government with effect from the first day of the agricultural year next following the date of publication of a notification in the official Gazette declaring that the Compensation Assessment-roll was finally published. 

 23. During the CS survey, the land was recorded as 'Nal'. With the passage of time when the bazaar in question expanded up to near the suit land, the recorded tenant might have made shops thereon for some quick bucks. With further extension of the bazaar, the shops might be now in the periphery of Ramchandrapur bazaar as claimed by defendant No.2. Land in the periphery cannot be deemed to be 'in the hat or bazaar' within the meaning of section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Such land was therefore never intended by the legislature to vest in the government under section 20(2a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. The defendant therefore, failed to produce any notification of final Compensation Assessment-roll vesting the suit land in the government.
